title: U.S. House · Arizona's 7th District
area: Southern and southwestern Arizona along the U.S.-Mexico border: most of Pima County (including much of Tucson), plus parts of Cochise, Yuma, La Paz and Maricopa counties.

context.text: Adelita Grijalva won a September 23, 2025 special election to fill the seat left vacant by the death of her father, Raúl Grijalva. House Speaker Mike Johnson did not swear her in until November 12, 2025 — 50 days after her election and, at 39 days as of late October, the longest gap between election and swearing-in in U.S. House history at that point. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes and Grijalva filed and then voluntarily dismissed a lawsuit over the delay.

candidates.name: Adelita Grijalva
candidates.ballotNote: Won a September 23, 2025 special election, then won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary unopposed.

summary.text: Adelita Grijalva is the Democratic incumbent U.S. Representative for Arizona's 7th Congressional District. A Tucson native, she worked for more than 25 years at Pima County Teen Court, served on the Tucson Unified School District Governing Board from 2002 and on the Pima County Board of Supervisors from 2020, and won the seat in a September 2025 special election after the death of her father, Rep. Raúl Grijalva. She is seeking a full term in 2026.

background.text: Grew up on the south side of Tucson with her two sisters and graduated from Pueblo High School, according to her official House biography; Wikipedia gives the year as 1989.
Earned a degree in political science from the University of Arizona (a B.A. in 1995, per Wikipedia).
Worked at Pima County Teen Court for more than 25 years, serving as its director; the program is a restorative juvenile diversion program for court-involved youth.

First elected to public office in 2002 to the Tucson Unified School District Governing Board, where she served about 18 years; she was the only board member to vote against ending the district's Mexican American Studies classes in 2012, according to Wikipedia.

Elected to the Pima County Board of Supervisors in 2020 and became the first Latina and second woman to chair the board, according to her official bio, which lists a county preschool program, affordable-housing investments and open-space protection among her accomplishments.
Daughter of the late U.S. Rep. Raúl Grijalva, whose Arizona's 7th District seat she won in the September 23, 2025 special election, defeating Republican Daniel Butierez Sr.
Sworn in on November 12, 2025, after a seven-week delay that followed the special election and coincided with a federal government shutdown, according to Wikipedia.
Serves on the House Committee on Education and Workforce and the Committee on Natural Resources and is a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and Congressional Hispanic Caucus.
Lives in Tucson with her husband Sol and has three children, according to her official bio.

positions.summary: Criticized the EPA's decision to roll back air pollution limits for fossil fuel power plants and called for moving forward on clean energy instead.
positions.quote: Instead of investing in cheaper clean energy solutions, Trump is propping up dirty and expensive fossil fuel plants in order to appease his donors. Arizonans deserve clean air and lower utility bills – not handouts to the coal industry. We should be moving forward on clean energy and stronger protections, not turning back the clock.

positions.summary: Co-introduced the Fund Schools, Not ICE Act, which would redirect ICE funding to Title I public schools and require DHS to sell recently purchased detention warehouse facilities.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce and the House Committee on Natural Resources (2025-2026).
Introduced the Fairness for Farm Workers Act, to expand overtime protections for agricultural workers under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

candidates.researchNotes: No completed Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey found. Positions above are drawn from her official House press releases; her House issues page (grijalva.house.gov/issues) lists topic areas without detailed statements.

summary.text: Daniel Butierez Sr. is the Republican nominee for Arizona's 7th Congressional District. Born in Tucson, he is a painting company owner who was the Republican nominee against Rep. Raúl Grijalva in 2024 and against Adelita Grijalva in the 2025 special election. According to his candidate survey, his campaign messages have centered on homelessness, border security and what he calls corruption in local government.

background.text: Born in Tucson, Arizona, in 1966, a third-generation Arizonan, according to his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey.
Career experience includes working as a contractor and construction worker; news coverage describes him as a painting company owner, and he says he owns two businesses.
Says he spent about 30 years pursuing legal relief after being imprisoned without what he describes as a valid conviction, until a judge ultimately ruled in his favor.
Was the Republican nominee in Arizona's 7th District in 2024, when he received more than one-third of the vote against Raúl Grijalva, according to CBS News.
Won the July 2025 Republican primary in the special election and lost the September 23, 2025 general election to Adelita Grijalva, 68.9% to 29.4%; he conceded shortly after results began coming in.
Describes a campaign plan to fund a program to help homeless people get back on their feet and to secure the border.
Advanced unopposed from the July 21, 2026 Republican primary with 21,934 votes.

priorities.text: Says securing the U.S.-Mexico border is central to his plans, including a proposed program to help homeless people and people struggling with drug use get back on their feet.
Says government too often 'throws money at a problem rather than a solution,' pointing to spending as a driver of inflation and higher interest rates.
Says he wants to bring attention to what he describes as corruption in local Tucson government.

positions.summary: Says securing the border is a focal point of his campaign.
positions.quote: Securing our Border: This is vital to my plans of helping our homeless get on their feet and drug users off of drugs.
